intro: This unit looks at places a town pays for: public parks, school gyms, and Friday night lights. Lincoln Park in Chicago is one public park. A school board approves gym money. Electric lights let games go after dusk.

Then the unit looks at rules you can say. A painted line is a short rule. IFAB writes the Laws of the Game. The Football Association met in London on 26 October 1863. The IHSA handbook lets Illinois schools meet. This course still does not teach plays.
bigQuestion: Who builds the rooms for play, and who writes the short rules that strangers share?

title: Our Field

chapters.title: Park, Gym, Lights
chapters.bigQuestion: Who pays for a school gym, a park field, and Friday night lights?

story.title: Lights Before the Crowd
story.kicker: Friday lights click on over an empty field before anyone arrives.
paragraphs: On Friday the field is empty at dusk. Then the lights come on. They hum. The grass turns bright green. No game has started yet.
Cars begin to park. A band warms up. The field belongs to the school district. Tax money and ticket sales help pay for the poles and the bulbs.
A child asks who owns the lights. The coach says the school owns them. The town helped pay for the poles. People share this field on Friday night.
This chapter names parks, gyms, and lights as civic rooms. Civic means people pay together so many people can use the place.
story.think: Who do you think paid for the gym or field nearest your school?

lessons.title: Parks Are for Sharing
lessons.mainIdea: A public park is land a city or park district keeps so many people can play.
reading: A *public park* is land held for everyone in a town. A park district or a city department mows it and makes rules for the fields.
Chicago opened Lincoln Park as public parkland in the 1800s. Other Illinois towns built parks later. The grass is not one family's yard.

words.d: land a city or park district keeps for everyone to use
a local office that runs parks and some gyms

look.title: Lincoln Park
look.text: Chicago's Lincoln Park grew from lakefront land set aside in the nineteenth century as a public park, not as a private club field.
look.cite: Chicago Park District history of Lincoln Park

choices: land kept for everyone in a town

check.q: Who may run local parks?

check.why: Cities and park districts run public parks.

lessons.title: Park Fields Have Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Park fields use posted rules so strangers can share the same grass.
reading: A park sign may say when lights go off. It may say which field is for soccer on Saturday. Those words help strangers share the grass.
Without a posted time, two teams might arrive at once. The sign is a small rule book nailed to a post.

words.d: a rule written on a sign where players can read it

look.title: The sign on the fence
look.text: Look at a metal sign on a chain-link fence. It lists field hours and which days soccer may use diamond two. Two coaches read it before they unload bags.
look.prompt: What problem does the sign try to stop?

check.why: Posted rules help strangers share one field.

check.q: What might a park sign tell you?
check.why: Signs may list hours and which field to use.

check.q: A posted rule is like
choices: a small rule book on a post
check.why: The reading compares the sign to a small rule book.

lessons.title: Who Pays for the Gym
lessons.mainIdea: A school gym is paid for by the school district, which uses public money.
reading: A school *gym* is a room the district builds. School boards approve the money. That money comes from taxes and other public funds.
The gym is not a private club. Classes use it in the day. Teams use it after school. The same floor serves both jobs.

words.d: an indoor school room built for class and games
the public body that runs the local schools and their buildings

look.title: A public building
look.text: Illinois public school buildings, including gyms, are built and repaired with district funds approved by a school board.
look.prompt: Why is a school gym different from a backyard hoop?

check.why: School boards approve district money.

check.q: When do classes use the gym?
check.why: Classes use it in the day; teams after school.

check.why: The gym belongs to the school district.

lessons.title: Naismith Needed a Gym
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball exists because a winter gym in Springfield needed an indoor game in 1891.
reading: James Naismith did not invent basketball on a park field. He invented it in a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in December 1891.
Winter had closed the outdoor fields. The gym was the only room his class had. The building shaped the game.

words.d: the teacher who invented basketball in a gym in 1891

look.title: Winter and a roof
look.text: Naismith's class at the International YMCA Training School needed a game that worked under a roof in winter, so he hung peach baskets in the gym.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941)
look.prompt: What would have been different if the class had met outside in July?

check.q: Where did Naismith invent basketball?
check.why: He invented it in a Springfield gym in 1891.

check.q: Why was the class indoors?
check.why: Winter kept the class inside.

check.q: What shaped the new game?
check.why: The building shaped the indoor game.

lessons.title: Lights Make Night Play Possible
lessons.mainIdea: Electric field lights let a town gather after dark for a school game.
reading: Before bright electric lights, outdoor games ended at dusk. Field *lights* let people play and watch after supper.
Many Illinois high schools light a football field on Friday night. The lights are part of the field, like the lines and the bleachers.

words.d: electric lamps that make an outdoor field usable after dark

look.title: Dusk and then glow
look.text: Look at a field at sunset. Players are hard to see. Then tall poles click on. The same grass becomes a night room for a town.
look.prompt: Who can come to a game once the lights work?

check.why: Outdoor games ended at dusk.

check.why: The reading names Friday night.

lessons.title: IHSA Games Use School Fields
lessons.mainIdea: IHSA football and other sports use school fields that towns already paid to build.
reading: The Illinois High School Association began in 1900. It schedules state series in many sports. Those games are played on school fields and in school gyms.
The IHSA does not own every field. Districts and towns own the buildings. The association writes the meet rules.

chapters.title: A Rule You Can Say
chapters.bigQuestion: Why does a short written rule help strangers play the same game?

story.title: Two Classes, One Line
story.kicker: Children from two classes meet at a painted line and both know what it means.
paragraphs: Recess. A second-grade line and a third-grade line reach the same white paint. No one planned a meeting. The line was already there on the blacktop.
A teacher says to stay behind the line until the whistle. Both classes hear the same sentence. The game can start without a long speech from anyone.
That sentence is a rule you can say. It is short. A child can repeat it. Strangers do not need a private code to begin. That is the point.
Sports leagues print longer books. The idea is the same as the painted line: say the rule so two towns can play one game.
story.think: What is one short rule you can say about a game at your school?

lessons.title: A Sentence Everyone Can Repeat
lessons.mainIdea: A useful playground rule is a short sentence children can say aloud.
reading: A good start rule is short. Stay behind the line until the whistle is one sentence. Children can repeat it to a friend.
Long secret codes do not travel. A short sentence travels from one class to the next class at recess.

words.d: words that tell how a game will be shared

look.title: Say it once
look.text: A teacher holds up one finger and says one sentence. Twenty children say it back. The line does not move. The words do the work.
look.prompt: Why might one sentence work better than a long speech at recess?

check.q: What makes a playground start rule useful?
choices: it is a short sentence children can say
it is written only in Latin
check.why: Short spoken rules travel.

check.q: What happens to long secret codes?
check.why: Long secrets do not travel.

check.q: Who can repeat a short rule?
check.why: Children can repeat a short sentence.

lessons.title: Lines Help Strangers
lessons.mainIdea: A painted line is a rule you can see, so people who just met can start together.
reading: A *line* on blacktop or grass is paint. It is also a rule. Stay behind it. Start on it. Do not cross it yet.
Two children who have never met can both use that line. They do not need to be friends first. The paint does the introducing.

words.d: a painted mark that shows where to stand or start

look.title: Paint as a sentence
look.text: Look at a white line on blacktop. No words are printed on it. Still, both classes treat it as wait here. The mark stands in for a sentence.
look.prompt: What sentence is the line saying?

check.q: What is a painted line in this lesson?
check.why: The line is a visible rule.

check.q: Do children need to be friends first to use the line?
choices: no, the paint works for strangers
check.why: Strangers can share a painted line.

check.q: The paint does the
check.why: The reading says the paint introduces the rule.

lessons.title: The Laws of the Game
lessons.mainIdea: Soccer's Laws of the Game are a printed book so clubs in many countries can use the same rules.
reading: The International Football Association Board, or IFAB, writes the *Laws of the Game*. Those laws are the world rule book for soccer.
A club in one country and a club in another country can play if they both use that book. The book does what the playground line does, at a larger size.

words.d: the official world rule book for soccer, written by IFAB

look.title: One book for many countries
look.text: IFAB publishes the Laws of the Game so matches in different countries can use the same numbered laws, including Law 3 on how many players and Law 5 on the referee.
look.cite: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 3 and Law 5
look.prompt: What problem does one world book try to solve?

check.q: Who writes the Laws of the Game?
check.why: IFAB writes soccer's world laws.

check.q: Why print the laws in a book?
choices: so clubs in many countries can use the same rules
check.why: A shared book lets distant clubs play.

check.why: Law 5 covers the referee.

lessons.title: 1863 Was a Meeting About Words
lessons.mainIdea: The Football Association met in London in 1863 to write one set of kicking rules.
reading: On 26 October 1863, clubs met in London. They formed the Football Association. They wanted one written game, not a different game on every green.
That meeting was about words on paper. The pitch came with the words. Without shared words, the rectangle would not mean the same thing in two towns.

words.d: the group formed in London in 1863 to write shared soccer rules

look.title: Freemasons' Tavern
look.text: The Football Association's first meeting was at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on 26 October 1863. The clubs came to agree on written rules for the kicking game.

check.q: The meeting was mainly about
check.why: It was a meeting about written rules.

lessons.title: IHSA Handbooks
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois high schools use IHSA by-laws and sport terms so state series can be fair.
reading: The IHSA publishes by-laws and sport terms. Schools that join agree to those words. That is how a school in Cairo and a school in Rockford can meet.
The handbook is not a playbook. It does not teach a formation. It says who may play and how a state series is run.

words.d: the written rules a school agrees to when it joins the IHSA

look.title: One state, one handbook
look.text: IHSA member schools follow the association's by-laws and the terms for each sport so regional and state series use the same eligibility and meet rules.

lessons.title: A Referee Carries a Book
lessons.mainIdea: By the late 1800s a soccer referee used a written law book, not only a spoken custom.
reading: Soccer's Laws of the Game gave the referee a written job. The referee starts play, stops play, and carries the laws onto the pitch.
IFAB still writes those laws. A referee in two countries can open the same numbered book.

words.d: the official who starts and stops a soccer match
the board that writes the Laws of the Game

look.title: Law 5
look.text: IFAB Law 5 says the referee enforces the Laws of the Game and may use a whistle so everyone hears the same decision.
